title: SVD and PCA: The Capstone: Visual Guide
outline: Title: SVD and PCA: The Capstone — six interactive visuals that build the singular value decomposition from A transpose A and then point it at data as PCA.

1. Manufacture The Symmetry | BRIDGE from the spectral theorem, which only fires on symmetric matrices, to A^T A. Drag the second column of a 3 x 2 matrix A and watch A^T A stay 2 x 2, stay symmetric with both off-diagonals equal to the column dot product a1.a2, keep every eigenvalue at or above zero, and show trace = sum of the squares of all entries; a test vector x proves x^T A^T A x = |Ax|^2, and the determinant readout flips between invertible and singular as the columns become dependent. | You never need a symmetric matrix to start with — the pattern X^T X manufactures one from any real A, and (A^T A)^T = A^T A needs only the reversal rule (MN)^T = N^T M^T.

2. Eigenvalues Become Sigmas | Sliders for the four entries of a 2 x 2 A (with presets [1 2 ; 2 1], [3 0 ; 0 4], [1 1 ; 1 1], [1 2 ; 3 4]) compute A^T A, its eigenvalues, the singular values as their square roots, the normalised eigenvectors as the columns of V, the rank as the count of nonzero sigmas, and u_i = A v_i / sigma_i; a toggle negates v2 and shows u2 flipping with it. | Sigma is the square root of lambda, not lambda — diag(9,16) gives singular values 4 and 3 — eigenvectors must be normalised before entering V, and the sign of a singular vector is genuinely free because u absorbs the flip.

3. Building U Columns | Sliders for m, n and rank r show U column by column: the first r come from the formula u_i = A v_i / sigma_i, the remaining m - r are filled from an orthonormal basis of the left null space N(A^T), with a live Sigma grid and counts for dim N(A^T) = m - r and dim N(A) = n - r; below, four candidate vectors are tested as the second column of U for the rank-1 case A = [1 1 ; 1 1]. | Count m, n and r first: the shortfall is always m - r, never n - r, and any orthonormal basis of N(A^T) will do — which is why two correct answers can differ.

4. Rotate Stretch Rotate | A four-stage stepper carries the unit circle through x, then V^T x, then Sigma V^T x, then U Sigma V^T x, with sliders for sigma1, sigma2 and the rotation angles of V and U; the marked directions travel from v1, v2 to the coordinate axes to the ellipse semi-axes along u1, u2, and setting sigma2 to zero flattens the plane onto a single line. | Orthogonal matrices change no length, so all the stretching lives in Sigma: the maximum stretch is sigma1 attained at v1, and the ellipse's axes point along the outputs u1 and u2, never along the inputs.

5. PCA By Hand | Four steps on three checkable points (1,1), (2,3), (3,2): center to get the mean (2,2), form C = (1/n) Xc^T Xc = [2/3 1/3 ; 1/3 2/3], eigendecompose for lambda = 1 and 1/3 with pc1 = (1,1)/sqrt2 and 75 % variance explained, then project a chosen point to get the score z = x.u, the rank-one rebuild x hat = z u and the residual; a shear slider moves all of it together. | PCA is the spectral theorem applied to a covariance matrix — and the reconstruction residual is always orthogonal to pc1, lying along the remaining eigenvector.

6. The Dependency Graph | The whole course as a directed graph where an edge from A to B means A requires B. Four modes recompute live: a topological build order by Kahn's rule, the transitive set a chosen component needs, the reverse-edge set that must be rebuilt if you change it, and an injected cycle (dot products -> PCA -> SVD -> A^T A -> dot products) that leaves the resolver with no valid first step. | Dependencies are transitive, forward edges are what you rest on and reverse edges are what breaks when you change something — and a cycle kills a build because no topological order exists at all.
